The '''Bregman method''' is an [[iterative algorithm]] to solve certain [[convex optimization]] problems involving [[Regularization (mathematics)|regularization]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last1=Xiong|first1=Kai|last2=Zhao|first2=Guanghui|last3=Shi|first3=Guangming|last4=Wang|first4=Yingbin|date=2019-09-12|title=A Convex Optimization Algorithm for Compressed Sensing in a Complex Domain: The Complex-Valued Split Bregman Method|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/336665179|journal=Sensors |publication-date=18 Oct 2019|volume=19|issue=20|page=4540|doi=10.3390/s19204540|pmid=31635423|pmc=6832202|bibcode=2019Senso..19.4540X|doi-access=free }}</ref> The original version is due to [[Lev M. Bregman]], who published it in 1967.<ref>Bregman L. "A Relaxation Method of Finding a Common Point of Convex Sets and its Application to Problems of Optimization". Dokl. Akad. Nauk SSSR, v. 171, No. 5, 1966, p.p. 1019-1022. (English translation: Soviet Math. Dokl., v. 7, 1966, p.p. 1578-1581)</ref>

The algorithm is a [[row-action method]] accessing [[constraint function]]s one by one and the method is particularly suited for large optimization problems where constraints can be efficiently enumerated{{Citation needed|date=April 2021}}. The algorithm works particularly well for [[Regularization (mathematics)|regularizers]] such as the <math>\ell_1</math> norm, where it converges very quickly because of an error-cancellation effect.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=Yin|first=Wotao|date=8 Dec 2009|title=The Bregman Methods: Review and New Results|url=https://www.caam.rice.edu/~optimization/L1/bregman/WotaoYin_Bregman_SIAMPDE_09.pdf|url-status=live|access-date=16 Apr 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100613215532/http://www.caam.rice.edu/~optimization/L1/bregman/WotaoYin_Bregman_SIAMPDE_09.pdf |archive-date=2010-06-13 }}</ref>

== Algorithm ==
In order to be able to use the Bregman method, one must frame the problem of interest as finding <math>\min_u J(u) + f(u)</math>, where <math>J</math> is a regularizing function such as <math>\ell_1</math>.<ref name=":0" />

The ''Bregman distance'' is defined as <math>D^p(u, v) := J(u) - (J(v) + \langle p, u - v\rangle)</math> where <math>p</math> belongs to the [[Subderivative|subdifferential]] of <math>J</math> at <math>u</math> (which we denoted <math>\partial J(u)</math>).<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=Bush|first=Jacqueline|date=10 Jun 2011|title=University of California, Santa Barbara Senior Thesis: Bregman Algorithms|url=https://web.math.ucsb.edu/~cgarcia/UGProjects/BregmanAlgorithms_JacquelineBush.pdf|url-status=live|access-date=16 Apr 2021|website=University of California Santa Barbara|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161130150743/http://web.math.ucsb.edu:80/~cgarcia/UGProjects/BregmanAlgorithms_JacquelineBush.pdf |archive-date=2016-11-30 }}</ref> One performs the iteration <math>u_{k + 1}:= \min_u(\alpha D(u, u_k) + f(u))</math>, with <math>\alpha</math> a constant to be chosen by the user (and the minimization performed by an ordinary convex optimization algorithm),<ref name=":0" /> or <math>u_{k + 1}:= \min_u(D^{p_k}(u, u_k) + f(u))</math>, with <math>p_k</math> chosen each time to be a member of <math>\partial J(u_k)</math>.<ref name=":1" />

The algorithm starts with a pair of primal and dual variables.  Then, for each constraint a [[Bregman divergence|generalized projection]] onto its feasible set is performed, updating both the constraint's dual variable and all primal variables for which there are non-zero coefficients in the constraint functions gradient.  In case the objective is strictly convex and all constraint functions are convex, the limit of this iterative projection converges to the optimal primal dual pair.{{Citation needed|date=April 2021}}

In the case of a [[basis pursuit]]-type problem <math>\min_{x: Ax = b}(|x|_1 + \frac{1}{2\alpha}|x|_2^2)</math>, the Bregman method is equivalent to ordinary [[gradient descent]] on the dual problem <math>\min_y (-b^t y + \frac{\alpha}{2}|A^t y - \text{Proj}_{[-1, 1]^n}(A^t y)|^2)</math>.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last=Yin|first=Wotao|date=28 May 2009|title=Analysis and Generalizations of the Linearized Bregman Method|url=ftp://ftp.math.ucla.edu/pub/camreport/cam09-42.pdf|journal=SIAM Journal on Imaging Sciences|volume=3|issue=4|pages=856–877|doi=10.1137/090760350|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170705134816/ftp://ftp.math.ucla.edu/pub/camreport/cam09-42.pdf|archive-date=2017-07-05|url-status=dead|access-date=16 Apr 2021}}</ref> An exact regularization-type effect also occurs in this case; if <math>\alpha</math> exceeds a certain threshold, the optimum value of <math>x</math> is precisely the optimum solution of <math>\min_{x: Ax = b}|x|_1</math>.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" />

== Applications ==
The Bregman method or its generalizations can be applied to:

* [[Image deblurring]] or [[Image denoising|denoising]]<ref name=":0" /> (including [[total variation denoising]]<ref name=":1" />)
* MR image{{Clarify|date=April 2021}} reconstruction<ref name=":0" />
*[[Magnetic resonance imaging]]<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|last1=Goldstein|first1=Tom|last2=Osher|first2=Stanley|date=2 Jun 2008|title=The Split Bregman Method for L1-Regularized Problems|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220124333|journal=SIAM J. Imaging Sci.|volume=2|issue=2|pages=323–343|doi=10.1137/080725891|access-date=22 Apr 2021}}</ref>
*[[Radar]]<ref name=":4" />
*[[Hyperspectral image|Hyperspectral imaging]]<ref name=":6" />
* [[Compressed sensing]]<ref name=":2" />
*[[Least absolute deviations]] or <math>\ell_1</math>-regularized linear regression<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last1=Boyd|first1=Stephen|last2=Parikh|first2=Neal|last3=Chu|first3=Eric|last4=Peleato|first4=Borja|last5=Eckstein|first5=Jonathan|date=19 Nov 2010|title=Distributed Optimization and Statistical Learning via the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers|journal=Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning|volume=3|pages=1–122|doi=10.1561/2200000016|citeseerx=10.1.1.722.981}}</ref>
*Covariance selection (learning a sparse covariance matrix)<ref name=":3" />
*[[Matrix completion]]<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal|last1=Huang|first1=Bo|last2=Ma|first2=Shiqian|last3=Goldfarb|first3=Donald|date=27 Jun 2011|title=Accelerated Linearized Bregman Method|journal=[[Journal of Scientific Computing]]|publisher=[[Plenum Press]]|publication-date=1 Feb 2013|volume=54|issue=2–3|pages=428–453|doi=10.1007/s10915-012-9592-9|arxiv=1106.5413|s2cid=14781930 |issn=0885-7474}}</ref>
*[[Structural risk minimization]]<ref name=":3" />

== Generalizations and drawbacks ==
The method has links to the [[method of multipliers]]  and [[dual ascent method]] (through the so-called ''Bregman alternating direction method of multipliers'',<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=Huahua|last2=Banerjee|first2=Arindam|date=13 Jun 2013|title=Bregman alternating direction method of multipliers|journal=NIPS'14: Proceedings of the 27th International Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems|volume=2|pages=2816–2824|arxiv=1306.3203}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite web|last=Jiang|first=Chunzhi|date=May 2015|title=Comparison of Variable Penalty ADMM with Split Bregman Method on Hyperspectral Imaging Problems|url=https://etda.libraries.psu.edu/files/final_submissions/9702|url-status=live|access-date=20 Apr 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200323014635/https://etda.libraries.psu.edu/files/final_submissions/9702 |archive-date=2020-03-23 }}</ref> generalizing the ''alternating direction method of multipliers''<ref name=":3" />) and multiple generalizations exist.

One drawback of the method is that it is only provably convergent if the objective function is ''strictly'' convex. In case this can not be ensured, as for [[linear program]]s or non-strictly convex quadratic programs, additional methods such as [[proximal gradient method]]s have been developed.{{Citation needed|date=April 2021}} In the case of the [[Total variation denoising#Rudin–Osher–Fatemi PDE|Rudin-Osher-Fatemi model]] of image denoising{{Clarify|date=April 2021}}, the Bregman method provably converges.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Jia|first=Rong-Qing|date=3 Oct 2008|title=Convergence analysis of the Bregman method for the variational model of image denoising|url=https://sites.ualberta.ca/~rjia/Paper06-10/JZZ09.pdf|journal=Applied and Computational Harmonic Analysis|publication-date=Nov 2009|volume=27|issue=3|pages=367–379|doi=10.1016/j.acha.2009.05.002|access-date=22 Apr 2021|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Some generalizations of the Bregman method include:

* Inverse [[scale space]] method{{Clarify|date=April 2021}}<ref name=":0" />
* Linearized Bregman<ref name=":0" />
* Logistic Bregman<ref name=":0" />
* Split Bregman<ref name=":0" />

=== Linearized Bregman ===
In the Linearized Bregman method, one linearizes the intermediate objective functions <math>D^p(u, u_k) + f(u)</math> by replacing the second term with <math>f(u_k) + \langle f'(u_k), u - u_k\rangle</math> (which approximates the second term near <math>u_k</math>) and adding the penalty term <math>\frac{1}{2\delta}|u - u_k|_2^2</math> for a constant <math>\delta</math>. The result is much more computationally tractable, especially in [[basis pursuit]]-type problems.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> In the case of a generic basis pursuit problem <math>\min \mu|u|_1 + \frac{1}{2}|Au - f|_2^2</math>, one can express the iteration as <math>v_{k + 1} := v_k + A^t(f - Au_k), u_{k + 1, i} := \delta~\text{shrink}(v_{k, i}, \mu)</math>  for each component <math>i</math>, where we define <math>\text{shrink}(y, a) := \begin{cases} y - a, & y\in(a,\infty) \\ 0, &y\in[-a, a]\\ y + a, & y\in(-\infty, -a) \end{cases}</math>.<ref name=":1" />

Sometimes, when running the Linearized Bregman method, there are periods of "stagnation" where the residual{{Clarify|date=April 2021}} is almost constant. To alleviate this issue, one can use the Linearized Bregman method with ''kicking'', where one essentially detects the beginning of a stagnation period, then predicts and skips to the end of it.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />

Since Linearized Bregman is mathematically equivalent to gradient descent, it can be accelerated with methods to accelerate gradient descent, such as [[line search]], [[Limited-memory BFGS|L-BGFS]], [[Barzilai-Borwein method|Barzilai-Borwein]] steps, or the [[Nesterov method]]; the last has been proposed as the ''accelerated linearized Bregman method''.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":7" />

=== Split Bregman ===
The Split Bregman method solves problems of the form <math>\min_u |\Phi(u)|_1 + H(u)</math>, where <math>\Phi</math> and <math>H</math> are both convex,<ref name=":1" /> particularly problems of the form <math>\min_u |\Phi u|_1 + |Ku - f|^2</math>.<ref name=":5" /> We start by rewriting it as the [[constrained optimization]] problem <math>\min_{u: d = \Phi(u)} |d|_1 + H(u)</math>, then relax it into <math>\min_{u, d} |d|_1 + H(u) + \frac{\lambda}{2}|d - \Phi(u)|_2^2</math> where <math>\lambda</math> is a constant. By defining <math>J(u, d) := |d| + H(u)</math>, one reduces the problem to one that can be solved with the ordinary Bregman algorithm.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":5" />

The Split Bregman method has been generalized to optimization over [[complex number]]s using [[Wirtinger derivatives]].<ref name=":4" />
